message: Context, so the answer fits our situation: a React component library built on styled-components v6 that prerenders every page to static HTML and hydrates it with the same components. Pieces of writing carry semantic classes put there by annotation objects: pd-* for what a piece of writing is (pd-paragraph, pd-code), pa-* for an annotation's mark (pa-table, pa-reference). A Format is an annotation that is itself a styled component and may replace the element it annotates (a Table replaces a section's element with its grid, whose column rules are generated inside it). One Theme component renders a single global sheet keyed on those classes and provides eight token values (font, size, leading, measure, space, ink, paper, link) through ThemeProvider. We are drawing the line between a component's own styles and that global sheet, and want to draw correctness from how the community already does it. Please answer with sources, the three main considerations for each part: (1) How do mature design systems in 2026 (for example Radix Themes, Chakra and Panda, MUI with Pigment CSS, shadcn on Tailwind, and a BEM-style system such as GOV.UK Frontend) divide component-local rules from global semantic-class rules, structure against skin and tokens against rules, and what fails when the line is drawn wrong (specificity wars, two authors of one property on one element, a theme coupled to every class)? (2) Should token values flow through ThemeProvider interpolations or through CSS custom properties written once by the theme, given server rendering and hydration parity, theme switching without regenerating classes, and where styled-components v6 and the broader ecosystem are heading? (3) Is there a recognised home for the rules a component's meaning requires regardless of theme, such as a parenthetical hidden, a blank invisible, or a closed page unseen: with the component that means it, or in the theme's sheet? (4) How do a semantic-class stylesheet and CSS-in-JS component styles coexist without collisions: cascade layers (@layer), injection order, naming convention, or something else, and what do design systems that mix the two actually do?
